passages.nngroup: Samhita Tankala and Katie Sherwin, 2 Feb 2024: 'Card sorting is a research method in which study participants place individually labeled cards into groups.' Open (most common), closed (validation; NN/g generally prefers tree testing for that), hybrid (NN/g generally advises against). Moderated vs unmoderated. 30-50 cards to avoid fatigue. At least 15 participants qualitative, 30-50 quantitative. Process: create cards, organize, label groups, analyze; pilot first; avoid repeating identical words across labels. Analysis: similarity matrix, standardization grid, dendrograms, plus moderated sessions for the why. Limits: no site context, one level of grouping, fatigue over 50 cards (big Miscellaneous pile), hard to interpret. Tree testing (reverse card sorting) evaluates an existing structure.
passages.wikipedia: Card sorting is a knowledge elicitation technique in which participants sort items into groups; used in UX design, information architecture and cognitive psychology. Open = generative, closed = evaluative, reverse card sorting = tree testing, modified-Delphi (Celeste Paul). Analysis: similarity/dissimilarity matrices feed hierarchical clustering (dendrograms) or multidimensional scaling; edit distance; Jaccard distance. Most useful when no accepted taxonomy exists or audiences group items differently. Cites Nielsen 1995 and 2004, Donna Spencer 2009 'Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories'.
passages.uxtweak: Body did not load via WebFetch (empty). From Ahrefs sitelinks: 'What is card sorting?', 'Card sorting and UX', tool CTA. Treated as a tool-vendor complete guide; covered by the same entities.
passages.nngroup-users: Jakob Nielsen, 18 Jul 2004, 'Card Sorting: How Many Users to Test': test 15 users; correlation with the full 168-user data set 0.75 at 5 users, 0.90 at 15, 0.95 at 30, 0.98 at 60; Tullis and Wood suggested 20-30; card sorting is generative so it needs more users than a qualitative usability test; do not build the structure from similarity scores alone.
passages.optimal-sequence: Optimal Workshop blog, 29 Mar 2016: tree test the existing IA first (baseline), run an open card sort, then tree test the proposed IA with the same tasks.
passages.userinterviews: 30-60 cards, 40 'sweet spot' (attributed to experts); at least 15 participants (NN/g); spreadsheet analysis method by Shanshan Ma; card sorts are generative and usually followed by tree tests.
passages.dovetail: Open/closed/hybrid table (who creates categories, best for, outputs: dendrograms, similarity matrices, results matrix, popular placements matrix); at least 15 qualitative, 30 quantitative; sessions of 5-30 minutes depending on card count.

outline.h2: What is card sorting in UX research?
outline.answerHint: Card sorting is a user experience (UX) research method in which participants group labeled cards, each naming one piece of content or one feature, into categories that make sense to them, so the team can build an information architecture (IA) that matches users' mental models.
points: Intro BEFORE this H2 (variety: 'one card, three piles'): open on a single card label from the worked example, e.g. 'Export billing history'. In an illustrative sort, some participants file it under Billing, some under Reports, some under Account. That split is the finding: the menu needs a cross-link or a new label. Then: keyword in the first sentence of the second paragraph at the latest (within 60 words), and one sentence on what the post gives (sort type choice, sample size, a 6-step runbook, how to read results, a worked example, tools, tree testing next).
UP link early (within the first 150 words): 'Card sorting is one of the six deliverables in our UX research services' -> /services/ux-research-services/ anchor exactly 'UX research services'.

Definition paragraph: parent = UX research; used to shape information architecture; name 'mental models'; one sentence on origin in knowledge elicitation (Wikipedia) and the standard book (Donna Spencer, 'Card Sorting: Designing Usable Categories', 2009; fact-checker confirms year). Use 'card sorting exercise' once. Answer 'Is card sorting qualitative or quantitative?' in one sentence here or FAQ 1: both, moderated sessions give reasons, large unmoderated samples give similarity scores.

Link UP to the pillar: one sentence placing card sorting among methods -> /blog/ux-research-methods/ anchor 'how card sorting fits among UX research methods' (CONDITIONAL: publishes today; remove if not live).

H3 'Which card sorting does this guide cover?' (disambiguation, PAA fold): one line each, everyday meaning first: sorting a deck or trading cards (card sorters, trays), sorting algorithms in computer science, the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test in neuropsychology, the Activity Card Sort in occupational therapy, classroom card sorts. Then: this guide covers the UX research method for menus and site structure. Keep to 5 short lines.

outline.h2: When does card sorting help your information architecture?
outline.answerHint: Card sorting helps when you must create or rebuild an information architecture and do not yet know how users group the content, for example a new product, a redesign, two products merging or a settings area that grew one item per release.
points: List of 4-5 situations (ul), each with why: new product with no taxonomy; redesign where the hub says navigation and IA were never tested; merging products or sites; content that different user groups label differently (Wikipedia: most useful when audiences group items differently); internal jargon in menus.

When it is the wrong method (ul, 3 items): users cannot find things in an existing menu -> tree test the current structure first; the problem is a task flow or a form -> usability testing; you need to know why users need the feature at all -> user interviews or contextual inquiry. Sideways link: 'contextual inquiry' -> /blog/contextual-inquiry/ anchor 'watching users work in their real setting' (only here; natural, method choice).
Limits (NN/g 2024): no site context, one level of grouping per sort, fatigue past 50 cards.
Close: if your redesign touches navigation, plan the card sort before wireframes.

outline.h2: Open, closed or hybrid card sorting, which fits your stage?
outline.answerHint: Open card sorting lets participants create and name their own groups, closed card sorting asks them to place cards into categories you set, and hybrid card sorting gives set categories but lets participants add new ones; pick by how much of the structure already exists.
points: Image: three-panel sort board (visual 1) right after the answer paragraph; text panel = table with rows: who names groups, best stage, question it answers, main output, typical analysis.
H3 'Open card sorting': discovery, new IA, learns users' words for groups; generative (Wikipedia); output similarity matrix + dendrogram + participant labels.

H3 'Closed card sorting': categories fixed (by business, regulation, existing product); checks whether cards land where expected; evaluative (Wikipedia); output results matrix / popular placements matrix; NN/g generally prefers tree testing for validating a structure - say so.
H3 'Hybrid card sorting': some categories fixed, others open; suits redesigns; NN/g generally advises against it because results mix two kinds of data, so say how to read new categories separately.
One sentence each on modified-Delphi card sorting (Celeste Paul; each participant refines the previous model; via Wikipedia) and reverse card sorting (= tree testing, forward reference to H2 9).

Decision tree visual (visual 2) at the end: 3 yes/no questions -> open / hybrid / closed / tree test instead. Keyword carrier: 'open vs closed' never as a stacked noun; write 'choosing between an open and a closed card sort'.

outline.h2: How many cards and participants does a card sort need?
outline.answerHint: A card sort needs 30-50 cards (NN/g) and at least 15 participants per user group for a qualitative study, or 30-50 participants for a quantitative one; our programme runs Optimal Workshop studies with 30-50 participants.
points: Cards: 30-50 cards to avoid fatigue (NN/g 2024); one level of granularity; no repeated words across labels (NN/g); plain user words, not internal codes; avoid labels that give the answer (the same word as a category).

Participants: Jakob Nielsen (NN/g, 18 Jul 2004) recommends 15; correlation with a 168-user data set 0.75 at 5, 0.90 at 15, 0.95 at 30, 0.98 at 60; Tullis and Wood suggested 20-30 (cited by Nielsen). Card sorting needs more users than a 5-user usability test because it is generative. Chart visual 3 (sample correlation curve) right after this paragraph; text panel = 4-row table.
Per user group: different groups (e.g. admins vs end users) each need their own sample; state this as the reason studies grow.

Our practice (hub): 30-50 participants per study in Optimal Workshop. Recruitment is its own 3-6 day step in our programme (hub). Soft lead line: recruiting 30-50 matched participants per group is where in-house sorts stall.
Respect CONFLICT 2 (print units).

outline.h2: How to run a card sorting study, step by step
outline.answerHint: To run a card sorting study, list the content, write 30-50 cards, choose the sort type and format, recruit participants, pilot the study, run it with follow-up questions and then analyze the groups.
points: Numbered list (ol) of 6 steps, our wording, not UXArmy's order: 1 content inventory and research question; 2 write and review cards (rules from H2 4); 3 choose sort type and format; 4 recruit and screen participants per user group; 5 pilot test with one colleague (NN/g) and fix confusing labels; 6 run and ask follow-up questions (why did this card go here, which cards were hard).
Runbook visual 4 (strip of 6 steps with the output of each step, no invented durations; note that in our programme the card sort and tree test sit inside the 4-8 day evaluative studies step).

H3 'Moderated or unmoderated, in person or remote?': table introduced by one sentence: moderated (think-aloud, reasons, smaller sample, about 60 minutes per dscout example) vs unmoderated (online, larger sample, 5-30 minutes per Dovetail), in person with index cards vs remote. Our practice: remote over Zoom and Optimal Workshop (hub FAQ). Answer 'remote card sorting' here.

H3 'Card sorting best practices' (PAA): 5 bullets in our own words, each one line: one research question per sort; plain labels; a 'not sure' pile allowed; pilot first; mix a few moderated sessions with the unmoderated sample (NN/g).
Lead line (MOFU): 'We run this as part of the evaluative studies step...' one natural invitation.

outline.h2: How do you analyze card sorting results?
outline.answerHint: Card sorting analysis looks at which cards participants put together (similarity matrix), how those pairs cluster into groups (dendrogram from hierarchical cluster analysis) and what participants called the groups, then checks the patterns against their comments.
points: Similarity matrix: each cell = share of participants who placed two cards in the same group (similarity score); explain how to read one row.
Dendrogram: built by hierarchical cluster analysis; where you cut it sets how many top-level groups you get; cut where the groups make sense to users and to the business, not at a fixed number.
Standardization grid (merge synonymous group names, e.g. 'Billing' and 'Payments') and, for closed sorts, the popular placements matrix (Optimal Workshop 101 guide names both).

Split cards: a card that lands in 2-3 groups needs a cross-link, a duplicate entry or a clearer label (example card from the intro). Combine with comments: Nielsen 2004 warns against building a structure from similarity scores alone.
Spreadsheet route for paper sorts: card x group count table, then percentages (userinterviews/dscout describe it; paraphrase, do not copy thresholds).
Annotated readout visual 5 (illustrative matrix excerpt + dendrogram with the cut line), text panel = what each mark means.

H3 'How is card sorting different from affinity mapping?' (PAA): card sorting = participants group content items to shape navigation; affinity mapping = researchers cluster their own notes and observations during synthesis. One link-free sentence (affinity mapping is a later post; plain text only).

Soft lead at the end: reading clusters next to session comments is where senior researchers earn their fee; our programme ends in a 90-minute readout (hub step 5). Deep link /services/ux-research-services/#how-does-the-ux-research-process-work anchor 'how our 5-step UX research process turns results into a readout'.

outline.h2: Card sorting example, regrouping a SaaS settings menu
outline.answerHint: In this illustrative card sorting example, 36 cards from a project-management app's settings menu go to an open card sort, and the results turn 9 scattered menu groups into 5 groups users recognize, with 2 cross-links for split cards.
points: Label clearly: 'Illustrative composite, not client data'. All numbers here are invented inputs for teaching; do not present them as research findings or client results.
Card list excerpt (8-10 of the 36 cards), the 3 main clusters, the split card from the intro, the resulting menu.
Before/after menu visual 6 (old 9 groups vs new 5 groups, cross-links marked); text panel = two lists.
End with one tree-test task that checks the new structure ('Where would you change who can see invoices?'), handing over to H2 9.
Do NOT name any client; do not say 'a client of ours'. The Seattle/San Francisco location page lines are capability statements, not cases.

outline.h2: Which card sorting tools fit open, closed and hybrid sorts?
outline.answerHint: Online card sorting tools for UX research, such as Optimal Workshop, Maze and Lyssna, run open, closed and hybrid sorts and produce the similarity matrix and dendrogram for you, while Miro boards and paper index cards suit small moderated sorts.
points: Table introduced by one sentence: tool, sort types, moderated/unmoderated fit, analysis outputs, free option. Fact-checker verifies each row on 2026-10-24 (plans, free tiers, whether each tool still offers hybrid sorts). No prices unless the fact-checker confirms them from the vendor page.

Rows: Optimal Workshop (our tool, hub; 'Optimal Card Sorting' on its product page, CONFLICT 4), Maze, Lyssna, UXtweak, Miro or FigJam boards (manual analysis), paper index cards. Free options answer the PAA 'good free card sorting tool' (freecardsort.com and template boards appear on page 1; fact-checker confirms before naming).
Selection rule: pick the tool by analysis output and recruiting panel, not by drag-and-drop UI.
Context word in every sentence that says 'card sorting tools' ('online', 'UX research'), because the 'card sorting tools' SERP also shows trading-card trays.

outline.h2: Why tree testing comes after card sorting
outline.answerHint: Card sorting proposes a structure from users' groupings and tree testing checks it, because tree testing (sometimes called reverse card sorting) asks participants to find items in a text-only version of the new menu.
points: Carrier: 'the card sorting vs tree testing question is about order, not choice'. Short comparison table (purpose, what participants do, method class, output) introduced by one sentence; NN/g (Tankala, 23 Feb 2024) for the difference.

Sequence (visual: IA research flow could replace visual 6 if the designer prefers; see visualsNote): tree test the current menu for a baseline, run an open or hybrid card sort, draft the new structure, tree test it with the same tasks (Optimal Workshop blog, 29 Mar 2016).

Example of a tree test task (PAA): reuse the task from H2 7; one sentence on what success and directness tell you. Keep tree testing to this H2 (future tree-testing post owns the deep how-to; plain text, no link).

Our practice (hub): card sort and tree test are one deliverable in Optimal Workshop inside the evaluative studies step; sibling hub fact: tree tests often use 10-15 tasks per test (web-app-design-services; may link that hub ONCE as the cross-hub link with anchor 'web app design services' where the tested structure becomes screens, or skip).

Main offer (MOFU): send us your current menu or sitemap and we will tell you in a free consultation which sort type and sample your structure needs; the full programme runs 4-8 weeks at $25,000-$60,000, and a programme with 1 user group, 10 interviews and 1 card sort sits near the low end (deep link to the hub cost section, anchor 'what a UX research programme with a card sort costs'). Second UP link here: /services/ux-research-services/ anchor 'UX research programme' (vary). Link /contact/ anchor 'send us your current menu or sitemap'.
4-6 questions as H3, first sentence = direct answer, boolean questions start Yes/No.

faqs.q: Is card sorting qualitative or quantitative?
faqs.hint: Both. Moderated sorts with 15 or so participants give reasons (qualitative); unmoderated sorts with 30-50 participants give similarity scores you can compare (quantitative). NN/g ranges. Same numbers as H2 4.

faqs.q: How long does a card sorting session take?
faqs.hint: About 5-30 minutes for an unmoderated online sort depending on the card count (Dovetail); a moderated session with follow-up questions runs longer, around an hour in dscout's example. Do not invent our own session length.

faqs.q: Can card sorting be done remotely?
faqs.hint: Yes. Remote card sorting runs in online tools such as Optimal Workshop, and moderated sessions run over video calls such as Zoom (hub FAQ wording). Remote loses some of the in-person conversation (Wikipedia), so add a few moderated sessions.

faqs.q: What are the limitations of card sorting?
faqs.hint: Card sorting shows how users group content but not whether they can find it in a real interface: no site context, one level of grouping per sort, fatigue past 50 cards (NN/g). Tree testing and usability testing cover the rest.

faqs.q: Should you run card sorting before or after wireframes?
faqs.hint: Before. Card sorting shapes the menu and site structure, which the wireframes then use; tree test the structure before high-fidelity design. Matches hub step order (evaluative studies before synthesis and design).

faqs.q: How many card sorts does a redesign need?
faqs.hint: Usually one sort per user group whose content differs, followed by a tree test; a second sort only when the first leaves large split groups. No invented counts; frame as rule of thumb from the method, not a statistic.
